The first time I learned to listen, it wasn’t in a classroom or a workshop. It happened in a quiet place where nothing demanded attention—an old neighborhood street at dusk, when the sky turns the color of worn denim and the air cools as if it’s exhaling. I was sitting on a curb with nowhere urgent to be, and I noticed that “silence” wasn’t an absence at all. It was a layered thing: distant traffic like a low ocean, a refrigerator hum from somewhere behind a curtain, the soft, rhythmic click of a ceiling fan settling into its evening pace. Even my own breathing became part of the soundtrack.

After that, listening changed my days. I started hearing the difference between noise and information. Noise is what leaks around edges—bright, restless, hard to hold. Information is what arrives with shape: the way a friend pauses before answering, the small shift in someone’s voice when they say they’re fine, the honest weight in a sentence that doesn’t try too hard.

I used to think attention was a kind of effort, something you wrestled into place. Now I think it’s more like trust. When you trust what’s in front of you, the world stops performing and starts speaking. And when the world speaks—whether through birds at sunrise or the steady creak of a porch swing—you realize you’ve been surrounded all along by messages you were simply too busy to notice.

So I keep practicing, one ordinary moment at a time.
